item.title: A case study in conflicts of interest | Science
item.description: In 2014, a paper—Nutt, et al—was published in the journal European Addiction Research that purported to evaluate the relative harms of 12 nicotine-containing products, based on a review by an expert panel. The materials assessed included conventional tobacco products, such as cigarettes, cigars, and pipes; traditional smokeless tobacco products, such as chewing tobacco and snuff; and manufactured nicotine replacement therapies (NRTs), such as patches, pouches, nasal sprays, and e-cigarettes (aka vapes). In the abstract, the authors concluded that “non-combusted sources of nicotine should be encouraged as the harms from these products are much lower.”

item.title: Advance more drugs for China’s aquaculture | Science
item.description: China operates the world’s largest aquaculture industry. In 2024, cultured aquatic production reached 60.6 million tonnes, accounting for 82.4% of national output and about 56% of global aquaculture production (1, 2). As farming intensifies and waters warm, disease outbreaks are becoming more frequent and complex, and farmers increasingly need effective, sustainable therapeutics that keep aquatic animals healthy and seafood safe for consumers. However, despite the industry’s scale, only 133 legally registered national-standard drugs and vaccines are available domestically for use in aquatic species (3), compared with about 2000 registered veterinary drugs for livestock and poultry (4). This portfolio cannot maintain the health and sustainability of China’s commercially farmed aquatic species.

item.description: Biophysicist Joseph Osmundson brings a scientist’s mind to a deeply personal subject in his genre-defying memoir, Spawning Season. This week on the Science podcast, Osmundson explores how queer parenthood intersects with themes present throughout the natural world, evoking questions about community and identity along the way.
